newsitem.title: CHINA: Gateway HK vulnerable to Asian corruption.
newsitem.headline: Gateway HK vulnerable to Asian corruption.

text.p: Multinational firms operating in Hong Kong looked on warily as the territory reverted to Chinese rule on Tuesday, fearing that mainland-style corruption could spread to here.
The big companies are adamant that they don't pay bribes in China and they don't condone corrupt practices.
"We have nothing to do with it and don't associate with it," Carlos Genardini, corporate vice president and general manager at Motorola, told journalists in Hong Kong last week.
"We're not saying that corruption doesn't exist, but there are a lot of honourable companies in China and we have been successful without engaging in corrupt practices," he said.
Ask any corporate executive and the answer is the same.

Yet survey after survey has found people doing business in Hong Kong, both foreigners and local Chinese, list the fear of increased corruption as one of their greatest worries now that Beijing has reasserted sovereignty over the British colony.
Bob Broadfoot of Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC) said such fears for Hong Kong are misplaced -- not because Hong Kong's corruption level is so low but because it isn't.
Broadfoot said that PERC's own corruption survey is flawed because in assessing Hong Kong it considers only fraud occurring within the territory and not cross-border corruption.
In its most recent survey, PERC gave Hong Kong a rating of 3.03 on a scale of zero to 10, with zero meaning least corrupt and 10 being the worst. It was the cleanest place in Asia next to Singapore.
China, in contrast, received a rating of 8.06. Indonesia, which is Asia's most corrupt, was just slightly higher at 8.67.
"A large part of Hong Kong's corruption problem has to do with cross-border corruption and that is not captured in the statistics at all," said Broadfoot.

For example, while Hong Kong doesn't have a huge problem with pirated software, many of the biggest pirates in southern China are Hong Kong Chinese who have crossed the border to take advantage of laxer controls.
In its role as a gateway not only to China but to other parts of Asia, Hong Kong is exposed to corrupt practices in other countries.

"I don't really worry about corruption carried out in Hong Kong, but as Hong Kong interfaces with the rest of Asia, to what extent do people in Hong Kong have to deal with the problem of corruption as it affects the rest of the region?" Broadfoot said.

Stephen Vickers, senior managing director of risk management firm Kroll Associates (Asia) Ltd, said it is up to companies to make sure they do not succumb to the lure of corruption in China, Hong Kong or anywhere else.
"Corruption will only increase if people want it to increase or acquiesce to it," he said.
But business executives concede that even the cleanest company can brush with corruption in doing business in Asia.
"We don't see much of a problem because we are a big company and countries want our business," said an executive of a major corporation with business operations throughout Asia.

"But there are times when we have to go through a high priced 'facilitator' to get to the right people. What he does with the money I don't know and I don't ask, but I suspect he splits it with the other parties," the executive said.
The low pay of civil servants in some Asian countries also encourages officials to take advantage of their status to line their own pockets, analysts said.
A World Bank report released last week found a direct correlation between low government pay and corruption.
"In Asia, there is no such thing as conflict of interest. Just interest," complained one businessman.
But some executives doing business in Asia said the region gets a bad rap when it comes to corruption.
"Corruption is not solely an Asian problem. It's not just an Asian issue, it's a business issue," said Jim McDonald, regional director, Asia-Pacific, for Marks & Spencer.
Cultural difference also play a role, analysts said.
In the West, expensive business dinners, lavish parties and all-expenses-paid golf outings are okay, but giving a fancy watch or luxury car to a government official is strictly out.
Asian business people may not see the difference.
"It's part of the culture. It's probably not perceived as corruption at all. It's just, I have my rice bowl, you have your rice bowl," said one manager.
